notes.meaning: God spoke to Moses in the Sinai desert during the first month of the second year after leaving Egypt. Chronologically, this happened a month before the census described in chapter 1, but it is recorded here to introduce the special Passover ruling that followed. Without this direct command from God, the Israelites would not have been required to observe the feast again until reaching Canaan.

God told Moses that the people of Israel must celebrate the Passover at its appointed season. Their first Passover in Egypt had been eaten in a hurry on the night they were delivered from slavery, but now they could celebrate it calmly and with better understanding. God wanted them to remember His rescue so they would not forget Him in the wilderness.

The feast was to take place at twilight on the fourteenth day of the month, exactly as God had previously instructed. The people were to follow every statute and ceremony, which included roasting a lamb and eating unleavened bread (bread made without yeast). This memorial reminded them of how the blood of the lamb had protected their families from judgment in Egypt.

Moses passed on God's words, and the entire nation kept the Passover at twilight on the fourteenth day in the wilderness of Sinai. They gathered the needed lambs and bread, doing everything just as the Lord had commanded Moses. This shows a season of willing obedience among the people before their later wanderings began.

A few men had become ceremonially unclean—temporarily unfit for sacred worship—by touching a dead body, likely while carrying out a burial. Since God's law forbade unclean people from sharing in sacred meals, they came to Moses and Aaron to ask why they had to miss the Lord's offering. They did not grumble against God's law, but genuinely grieved that circumstances kept them from worship. It is a good sign when our hearts long for God's ordinances and sorrow when we are hindered from them.

Moses did not rush to make up his own answer, but told the men to wait while he inquired of the Lord. He showed great humility by taking this difficult case directly to God for guidance. Church leaders should likewise seek God's direction through His word and prayer rather than relying on their own opinions.

The Lord replied with a gracious rule that would apply to Israel for all future generations. If anyone became unclean by touching a corpse, or was away on a distant journey, they were still expected and permitted to celebrate the Passover. God provided a way for those with unavoidable hindrances so they would not be left out of covenant worship.

God instructed that those who had been prevented were to observe the Passover exactly one month later, on the fourteenth day of the second month at twilight. They were still required to eat the lamb with flat unleavened bread and bitter herbs. This second chance showed God's kindness to those who sincerely wanted to worship Him but were stopped by circumstances beyond their control.

The make-up Passover was not a watered-down ceremony, but had to follow all the regular rules of the feast. They could not leave any meat until the morning, nor could they break any of the lamb's bones. While God mercifully accommodated their schedule, He did not lower His holy standard for how the sacrifice was to be honored.

If a person was clean and not away on a journey, yet chose to skip the Passover, that person was to be cut off from God's people. Neglecting God's feast out of carelessness or defiance was a grave sin that brought severe judgment. God graciously pardons those who are genuinely hindered, but He does not tolerate deliberate disregard for His commands.

Any foreigner living among the Israelites was also allowed to keep the Passover, as long as they obeyed all of its rules. This meant entering the covenant community through circumcision before partaking of the feast. There was to be one standard for both the native-born Israelite and the foreigner, pointing forward to God's plan to welcome all nations into His kingdom.

On the day the tabernacle was set up, a miraculous cloud covered the tent, and from evening until morning it looked like fire. This cloud was the visible sign of God's presence and protection over His people. It showed that the Lord had truly come to live among them in the wilderness.

The miraculous covering remained over the tabernacle continually, appearing as a cloud by day and as fire by night. A plain cloud would not be seen in the dark, and fire would be hard to see in the bright desert sun. By providing both, God gave Israel constant, visible proof that He was watching over them around the clock.

Whenever the cloud lifted up from the tabernacle, the Israelites packed their camp and set out on the journey. Wherever the cloud came to a stop and settled down, that was where they set up their tents. God Himself acted as their guide, directing every step of their journey through the desert.

The Israelites traveled only when the Lord commanded, and they camped only when the Lord commanded. The movement of the cloud was the visible way God made His will known to the nation. As long as the cloud rested over the sacred tent, the people remained right where they were.

Even when the cloud stayed in one spot for many days, the Israelites obeyed the Lord's charge and did not move. Though they were eager to reach the Promised Land, they learned to wait patiently for God's sign. Believers lose no time when they are quietly waiting for God's time.

Sometimes the cloud stayed for just a few days, or only from evening until morning, while at other times it lingered for two days, a month, or a whole year. Regardless of how long or short the stay was, the people moved only when the cloud lifted. This unpredictable rhythm kept Israel completely dependent on God, always ready to follow His lead on short notice.

Every movement of the camp happened at the Lord's command through Moses, and the people faithfully obeyed His charge. The author repeats this point several times to emphasize Israel's trust and obedience during this stage of their journey. Walking with God means surrendering our own plans and letting Him choose when we rest and when we move forward.
